status: drafted by direct reading of the real extracted Ethiopian-translation verse text (Assets/Resources/Verses/Ethiopian/esther_21.json, single-pass), structurally cross-checked verse-by-verse against the book's own 10-chapter/167-verse layout; consulted the existing KJV Esther.json only for tier-naming style, not copied blindly
notes:
Real structural finding, worth flagging clearly: this Ethiopian-translation source text for Esther is NOT the extended/Greek-Additions form of Esther (with Mordecai's dream, Esther's prayer in the throne-room scene, the full text of the king's letters, etc.) that many Orthodox-canon Bibles carry for this book. The extracted text here is the standard 10-chapter, 167-verse Hebrew/Masoretic-structure Esther (verified by direct chapter-by-chapter verse count: 22+23+15+17+14+14+10+17+32+3=167, matching exactly), and its wording is effectively identical to the familiar English (KJV-style) rendering of Esther, unlike this same Ethiopian source's genuinely distinct content elsewhere in the canon (e.g. its 9-chapter 'Ezra' matching the 1 Esdras tradition). This is reported as an observed fact about the source file, not assumed from memory - don't 'correct' it to match an expected extended-canon shape.

Character/tier structure: 5 person-type manager tiers + 1 law-type tier, same shape as the existing KJV Esther index, because the underlying narrative content in this specific extracted text is the same standard-canon story beat-for-beat. Ids are suffixed '_ethiopian' throughout specifically to avoid collision with the existing KJV CharacterIndex ids for the same names (per the project's cross-translation id rule).

Naming-collision flags carried forward from direct reading of this text: 'Ahasuerus' (1:1) is a royal name/title also used elsewhere in scripture for other rulers (Ezra 4:6, Daniel 9:1) - not asserted to be the same figure. Two royal chamberlains conspire together and are always named as a pair, never differentiated individually (2:21, spelled 'Bigthan'; 6:2 spells the same figure 'Bigthana' - a spelling variant within this same source text, not a different person) - kept as one paired submanager entry rather than invented as two. Harbona (1:10) and Harbonah (7:9) are likewise the same figure under a spelling variant within this text.

Genealogy hedges applied per the established methodology: Mordecai's descent 'the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite' (2:5) is stated text, but any further identification of this Kish with Saul's father Kish is a traditional/scholarly inference never made by the text itself - not asserted here. The antecedent of 'who had been carried away' (2:6) - Kish or Mordecai himself - is genuinely ambiguous in this text and left unresolved rather than guessed. Haman's title 'the Agagite' (3:1, 3:10, 8:3, 8:5, 9:24) is never explicitly linked by this text to King Agag of 1 Samuel 15 - noted as a thematic/traditional association only. Zeresh's maternity of Haman's ten named sons (9:7-10) is the natural implication of being 'his wife' (5:10) but is not stated outright by the text, so it is noted as implied rather than asserted as fact.

Schema self-check performed: every scribeTiers[].managerId (ahasuerus_ethiopian, vashti_ethiopian, esther_ethiopian, mordecai_ethiopian, haman_ethiopian, purim_ethiopian_esther) resolves to a real characters[].id. Every characters[].parentManagerId (ahasuerus_ethiopian, esther_ethiopian, haman_ethiopian) resolves to a real manager id. purim_ethiopian_esther's deliveredBy resolves to mordecai_ethiopian. No character holds both a scribeTier and a parentManagerId. The characters array is fully populated (12 entries: 5 person managers, 6 submanagers, 1 law tier).

characters.name: Ahasuerus
characters.genealogyNote: No parentage or children stated in this text. Reigns 'from India even unto Ethiopia, over an hundred and seven and twenty provinces' (1:1) - the same span of provinces recurs verbatim at 8:9. 'Ahasuerus' is reused elsewhere in scripture as a royal name/title for other rulers (e.g. Ezra 4:6, Daniel 9:1); not asserted to be the same man here.

verses.note: Introduced reigning over 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia; holds a 180-day display of his kingdom's riches in his third year.
Sends seven chamberlains to bring Queen Vashti before the feast to show her beauty; she refuses, and his anger burns.
Loves Esther above all the women and sets the royal crown on her head in his seventh year, making her queen instead of Vashti.
Gives his own ring to Haman, telling him the silver and the people are his to do with as he pleases.
Rises in wrath from the wine banquet after Esther names Haman as the enemy; orders Haman hanged on Haman's own gallows.
Gives Mordecai the ring taken back from Haman and grants Esther and Mordecai authority to write a new decree in his name.

funFacts: This book never names God directly anywhere in its ten chapters, a distinction unique among the books indexed so far.

characters.name: Memucan
characters.perkNote: The one prince among the seven who actually speaks - proposes the specific wording of the decree removing Vashti (1:16-21), turning the king's anger into formal royal policy.
characters.genealogyNote: Named as one of 'the seven princes of Persia and Media, which saw the king's face, and which sat the first in the kingdom' (1:14); no further genealogy given.

verses.note: Named among the seven princes consulted by the king on what law applies to Vashti's refusal.
Answers that Vashti's act will spread contempt to husbands throughout the provinces, and proposes the irrevocable decree against her; the king and princes are pleased and act on his word.

characters.name: Bigthan and Teresh
characters.perkNote: Two door-keeping chamberlains whose exposed plot against the king becomes the unpaid debt the chronicles later repay through Mordecai's public reward (ch. 6) - a threat removed rather than support given.
characters.genealogyNote: Always named as a pair, 'two of the king's chamberlains... of those which kept the door' (2:21); the text never differentiates between them individually, so they are kept as one paired entry. Spelled 'Bigthan' at 2:21 and 'Bigthana' at 6:2 within this same source text - a spelling variant, not a second person.

verses.note: Grow wroth and seek to lay hand on King Ahasuerus; Mordecai learns of it and reports it through Esther; both are found out and hanged, and it is written in the book of the chronicles.
The chronicle entry naming 'Bigthana and Teresh' is read back to the sleepless king, setting up Mordecai's reward.

characters.name: Vashti
characters.genealogyNote: No parentage or children given. Her fate after being deposed is not stated beyond losing her royal position (1:19) - the text does not say she was executed or banished.

verses.note: Makes her own feast for the women in the royal house, running alongside the king's much larger feast for the men.
Refuses to come at the king's commandment brought by his chamberlains.
Memucan's proposed decree: Vashti is not to come before the king again, and her royal estate is given to another woman 'better than she.'
Once his wrath is appeased, the king remembers Vashti and what was decreed against her.

characters.name: Esther
characters.genealogyNote: Named daughter of Abihail (2:15, referenced again 9:29); mother not named. Esther is Mordecai's cousin by blood, 'his uncle's daughter' (2:7), not his biological daughter - orphaned, she was 'taken for his own daughter' by Mordecai, an adoptive relationship the text states explicitly rather than a literal parent-child one.

verses.note: Introduced as Hadassah, that is Esther, orphaned and fair, taken by Mordecai as his own daughter after her parents' death.
Keeps her Jewish people and kindred hidden at Mordecai's charge, both before and after becoming queen.
The king loves her above all the women and sets the royal crown on her head, making her queen instead of Vashti.
Calls for a three-day fast among the Jews of Shushan before approaching the king unbidden: 'if I perish, I perish.'
Stands in the inner court in her royal apparel; the king holds out the golden sceptre to her.
Petitions for her life and her people's lives, naming Haman directly as 'the adversary and enemy... this wicked Haman.'
Writes with Mordecai 'with all authority' a second letter confirming the observance of Purim, which is written in the book.

funFacts: Esther carries two names in this text: 'Hadassah,' introduced first, and 'Esther,' used throughout the rest of the book (2:7).

characters.name: Hegai
characters.perkNote: Keeper of the women who favors Esther immediately, giving her preferential preparation, seven chosen maidens, and the best place in the house of the women (2:9).
characters.genealogyNote: Identified only by office, 'keeper of the women' (2:3, 2:8). A separate chamberlain, Shaashgaz, later keeps the house of the concubines (2:14) - a different office and a different person.

verses.note: Esther comes into his custody; she pleases him and he speedily grants her purification items, seven chosen maidens, and the best place in the house of the women.
When her turn comes to go before the king, Esther requires nothing but what Hegai the keeper of the women advises.

characters.name: Hatach
characters.perkNote: The chamberlain appointed to attend Esther; carries the copy of Haman's decree and Mordecai's charge to her, then carries her reply back (4:5-17), making him the message-relay that turns Mordecai's warning into Esther's decision to act.
characters.genealogyNote: Identified only by office, 'one of the king's chamberlains, whom he had appointed to attend upon her' (4:5).

verses.note: Sent by Esther to Mordecai to learn the cause of his mourning; brings back the copy of the destruction decree and Mordecai's charge that she plead for her people.
Carries Esther's reply back to Mordecai, that none may approach the king unbidden without risking death unless the golden sceptre is extended.

characters.name: Mordecai
characters.genealogyNote: Genealogy per 2:5: 'the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite.' Whether this Kish is the same Kish who fathered King Saul is never stated by the text - a traditional/scholarly inference only, not asserted here. Whether the 'carried away' clause in 2:6 refers to Kish or to Mordecai himself is genuinely ambiguous in this text and left unresolved. Raises his orphaned cousin Esther as his own daughter (2:7), but she is not his biological child, so she is not listed under 'children.'

verses.note: Introduced by genealogy - son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjamite - carried away from Jerusalem with the captivity of Jeconiah king of Judah.
Brings up Hadassah, that is Esther, his uncle's daughter, taking her as his own daughter after her parents' death.
Learns of Bigthan and Teresh's plot and reports it through Esther in his own name; it is written in the book of the chronicles.
Alone among the king's servants at the gate, refuses to bow or do reverence to Haman.
Sends word to Esther that deliverance will arise for the Jews from some place even if she stays silent, and asks whether she has come to the kingdom 'for such a time as this.'
Is dressed in royal apparel and led on horseback through the city by Haman himself, then returns to the king's gate.
Receives the king's ring taken back from Haman and goes out in royal apparel of blue and white with a great crown of gold.
Ends the book next in rank to King Ahasuerus, great among the Jews, seeking the good of his people and speaking peace to all his seed.

characters.name: Haman
characters.genealogyNote: Called 'the Agagite' throughout (3:1, 3:10, 8:3, 8:5, 9:24); this text never states a direct genealogical link to King Agag of 1 Samuel 15, only the title - any such link is a thematic/traditional association, not stated fact. His ten sons are named only as a list of the slain and later hanged (9:7-10) with no individual action, so they are treated as a group in genealogyLists rather than invented as individual characters.

verses.note: Promoted by the king above all the princes, described as 'Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite.'
Full of wrath at Mordecai's refusal to bow, scorns laying hands on Mordecai alone and instead plots to destroy all Jews throughout the kingdom.
Casts Pur (the lot) to set the date of destruction and offers ten thousand talents of silver to fund the decree.
Boasts to Zeresh and his friends of his riches and honor, but says it profits him nothing while Mordecai sits unbowed at the gate; they counsel him to build a fifty-cubit gallows.
Named by Esther as 'this wicked Haman,' found fallen on Esther's own bed pleading for his life, and hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.
His ten sons are slain by the Jews in Shushan; the Jews take no spoil.

characters.name: Zeresh
characters.perkNote: Haman's wife and closest counsel - first proposes the gallows for Mordecai (5:14), then later warns Haman his fall before Mordecai is now certain (6:13).
characters.genealogyNote: Described simply as Haman's wife (5:10). The text does not explicitly state she is the mother of his ten named sons (9:7-10), though it is the natural implication - noted as implied, not stated.

verses.note: Haman recounts his grievances to her and his friends; she and they advise a fifty-cubit gallows for Mordecai, which pleases Haman.
After Mordecai is publicly honored, Zeresh and Haman's wise men tell him he will surely fall before a man of Mordecai's seed.

characters.name: Harbona
characters.perkNote: Speaks up at the critical moment to point the king toward the gallows Haman built for Mordecai, directly causing Haman's execution method (7:9-10).
characters.genealogyNote: Named among the seven chamberlains who served before the king (1:10, spelled 'Harbona'); the same figure speaks again at 7:9, spelled 'Harbonah' within this same text - a spelling variant, not a different person.

verses.note: Named among the seven chamberlains who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus.
Tells the king of the gallows standing at Haman's house, built for Mordecai who had spoken good for the king; the king orders Haman hanged on it.

characters.name: The Institution of Purim
characters.purpose: Establishes an annual two-day feast (the 14th and 15th of Adar) commemorating the Jews' deliverance from Haman's planned massacre, turning the month 'from sorrow to joy, and from mourning into a good day' (9:22) into a lasting yearly memorial 'throughout every generation, every family, every province, and every city' (9:28). Named after the Pur (the lot) Haman cast to fix the date of the intended destruction (9:24-26), so the very device meant to destroy the Jews gives its name to the feast celebrating their survival.

verses.note: Explains why Jews in unwalled towns keep the 14th of Adar, while Shushan (where the fighting ran an extra day) keeps the 15th.
Mordecai writes letters to all the Jews in the king's provinces establishing the 14th and 15th of Adar as annual days of feasting, gladness, and gift-giving to the poor.
Explains the feast's name, Purim, from Pur, the lot Haman cast against the Jews.
Esther, with Mordecai, writes a second letter with full authority confirming the observance for all generations, and it is written in the book.

genealogyLists.note: Bulk/unresolved references, kept out of the character list above per the established methodology.

seven_princes_of_persia_and_media_esther.note: Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, and Marsena - named as a group with no individual differentiation. Memucan, the seventh of the group, IS individually differentiated (he speaks at 1:16-21) and has his own character entry.

seven_chamberlains_esther_1_10.note: Mehuman, Biztha, Bigtha, and Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas - named as a group with no individual differentiation. Harbona, the seventh named, IS individually differentiated later (he speaks in ch. 7) and has his own character entry.

shaashgaz_esther_2_14.note: Keeper of the house of the concubines - a different office from Hegai, keeper of the virgins. Named once with no individual action beyond his office.

hamans_ten_sons_esther_9_7-10_and_9_13-1.note: Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha, Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha, Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vajezatha - named only as a list of the slain, then again as hanged; no individual differentiation or action beyond the name.
